# Zero Framework LLM Documentation

This is the main agent-facing documentation bundle for Zero. It should be
loaded before planning or coding a Zero app. It intentionally repeats the most
important framework docs in one file so agents use Zero's existing surfaces
instead of rebuilding them.

Use this file first. Use the linked docs for deeper subsystem details.

## Product Summary

Zero is a Bun/Elysia full-stack app framework for building serious web apps
quickly from one integrated platform. It combines:

- Bun and Elysia server runtime
- React frontend runtime
- file-router pages, layouts, route groups, and route auth metadata
- ReactiveDB over SQLite
- ReactiveDB Fabric for bounded actor-owned file/WAL, hot, and hybrid
  multi-database topologies (active unreleased feature-branch work)
- WebSocket sync and lazy `/api/data`
- generated resource CRUD with server-side policy
- auth, email, account lifecycle, password reset/setup, email verification,
  and optional MFA
- installed desktop/mobile/extension OpenID Connect auth with Authorization
  Code + PKCE, with release status varying by client SDK
- storage, public upload grants, and storage management UI
- workflows, scheduler, rooms, presence, notifications, state sync
- platform tokens for one-time and resumable public flows
- observability codes/sinks and protected event routes
- AI provider layer, tool helpers, conversations, embeddings, speech,
  transcription, image generation
- zvec-backed vector storage
- browser-grade HTML/CSS-to-PDF rendering with direct storage composition
- migrations, schema history, rollback safety, backups, and drift planning
- reusable hooks, app shells, admin organisms, data tables, master-detail,
  Kanban, public page components, and animated icon/UI primitives

Zero's integrated identity, session, tenancy, and authorization subsystem is
called **Guardian**. Guardian is documentation/product vocabulary only: keep
using the established `auth.*` configuration, `/auth/*` routes, and
`@zero/framework/auth` APIs.

Zero's app-building rule is simple: **use framework pieces first**. Do not
recreate auth forms, modal managers, storage browsers, data tables, sidebars,
app shells, hooks, CRUD/sync plumbing, or backend service wiring unless the
framework surface is genuinely missing.

Current unreleased-candidate boundary:

- This unreleased tree implements `single/simple`, `single/advanced`,
  `multi/simple`, and `multi/advanced` through one app-local runtime and
  authorization kernel. Omitted capability axes still resolve to
  `single/simple`. Treat the new profiles as a release candidate until the
  implementation and cross-cutting release gates pass.
- Auth-enabled `createApp()` installs Bearer-required Sync plus private/scoped
  framework-table policy. Direct `createSyncPlugin()` is a lower-level,
  public/allow-all primitive unless the app explicitly supplies auth and policy.
- Managed ephemeral and presence topics use server-owned user/tenant
  namespaces, and room topics revalidate membership. Raw/custom Sync
  compositions must supply equivalent policy and cannot treat a caller topic
  or room ID as authority.
- The TypeScript `@zero/framework/native` core is implemented in this package.
  The separate Rust/Tauri and Chrome MV3 repositories are functional private
  `0.0.0` previews; none is a released package.
- Auth services are app-local and isolated across concurrent runtimes. Legacy
  no-argument `get*` helpers are compatibility adapters only and fail when no
  unambiguous runtime exists.
- Opt-in verified-company-domain request admission and the bounded append-only
  authorization/control-plane audit are implemented in this unreleased tree.
  Multi-mode bootstrap also creates a protected Administration Organization;
  strict browser SDK/hooks and packaged controls cover its people and the
  capability-gated customer-organization directory/lifecycle. Break-glass
  support, tenant-custom roles, broader populated-app discovery/migration
  tooling beyond exact pre-024 administration reconciliation,
  domain autojoin/aliases/direct transfer, and upstream enterprise SSO remain
  separate future capabilities. File-mode runtimes sharing one SQLite database
  relay durable row and State Sync changes and poll durable auth authority so
  another runtime's security change promptly revalidates local sockets and
  managed ephemeral bindings. This is not replication for `hot`/`ephemeral`
  databases, separate database files, cross-host messages, or RAM-only
  ephemeral topic values. Registered resources now use explicit server-owned
  client exposure plus optional immutable read/create/update/filter/sort field
  allow-lists. Under shared-row isolation, multi-mode startup validates actual
  non-partial tenant-leading indexes, tenant-scoped business uniqueness, and
  tenant-consistent composite foreign keys between registered tenant
  resources; physical tenant isolation validates the actor realm instead.
- ReactiveDB Fabric is implemented on an unmerged child feature branch, not a
  released app contract. It keeps the historical control/auth database pinned
  and can route physical tenant Resources to isolated actor-owned databases
  selected only from trusted authorization scope. Generated Resource CRUD,
  lazy data reads, and one multiplexed WebSocket use that topology. File/WAL
  databases have independent subprocess writer lanes and optional read lanes;
  bounded hot placement and synchronous hybrid selection are implemented with
  explicit durability contracts. Read the architecture document before using
  or changing this surface; fleet lifecycle, operator-grade backup/restore,
  online placement migration, and the full package/OS matrix remain release
  gates.

Read [Releasing Zero](docs/releasing.md) before describing a capability as
publicly supported.

  security, storage composition, workflows, errors, and adapters.

  for the four-profile auth system; it separates implemented and planned
  capability.
- `docs/auth/multi-tenant-auth-implementation-checklist.md`: authoritative
  delivery gates for the unreleased multi-tenant/advanced-auth runtime.
- `docs/auth/application-access-administration.md`: implemented
  single/advanced application-role administration contract.
- `docs/auth/tenant-member-administration.md` and
  `docs/auth/tenant-invitations-and-join-requests.md`: implemented active-tenant
  control-plane, SDK, hook, and packaged UI contracts.
- `docs/auth/verified-domain-onboarding.md`: implemented exact-domain DNS plus
  mailbox-proof request-to-join contract and deliberate v1 exclusions.
- `docs/auth/control-plane-audit.md`: implemented bounded append-only
  authorization/security audit, query/export, retention, hook, and viewer.
- `docs/auth/auth-data-plane-capability-matrix.md`: enforcement owner, live
  scope source, focused evidence, and trusted escape hatch for every official
  access-surface family.
- `docs/auth/browser-authorization.md`: implemented browser-safe live
  authorization projection and visibility-gate contract.
- `docs/stabilization-plan.md`: historical stabilization snapshot, not the
  current release gate.
- `docs/doctor-usage-audit-plan.md`: planned doctor checks for catching app
  code that bypasses Zero APIs/components/services.

## Historical And Working Design

- `docs/auth/multi-tenant-sso-rbac-working-design.md`: temporary detailed audit
  and implementation rationale. It intentionally preserves pre-implementation
  findings and proposed language; it is not an authoritative current API or
  release contract.

## Engineering Rules For Agents

- Read relevant docs before changing code.
- Use `@zero/framework/*` public imports in package-mode apps.
- Keep app code outside framework source: `app/`, `server/`, `db/schema.ts`,
  `zero.config.ts`.
- Keep `app/server.ts` thin: import config, call `createApp(config)`, listen.
- Put platform config in `zero.config.ts`.
- Backend routes should be thin. Business logic belongs in services or small
  helper modules.
- Security decisions must be server-side. Frontend gates are UX only.
- Use Elysia best practices: Elysia instances as controllers/plugins,
  validation models as runtime/type source of truth, explicit dependencies,
  named plugins when deduplication matters, and lifecycle scope intentionally.
- Do not pass full Elysia `Context` into generic services. Destructure and pass
  only what the service needs.
- Prefer Zero observability for logs, warnings, caught errors, and lifecycle
  events.
- Prefer Zero UI components over raw HTML controls.
- Do not make one-off palettes. Use design tokens.
- Keep reusable UI as components/organisms, not forced pages.
- Update docs when behavior changes.

## Local Create Workflow

Inside this framework checkout, create a local package-mode app:

```sh
bun run install:local-tools
zero-new ../my-zero-app
cd ../my-zero-app
bun run dev
```

Without the local convenience wrapper:

```sh
bun run create-zero -- ../my-zero-app --local --install
cd ../my-zero-app
bun run dev
```

`--local` packs the current checkout with the package publish allowlist, stores
the archive under the generated app's ignored `.zero/framework/` cache, and
writes that archive as the `@zero/framework` dependency. This prevents direct
source linking, duplicate React runtimes, and checkout-only file exposure.
`--install` runs `bun install` after scaffolding.

Without install:

```sh
bun run create-zero -- ../my-zero-app --local
cd ../my-zero-app
bun install
bun run dev
```

Published package shape later:

```sh
bunx -p @zero/framework create-zero my-zero-app
cd my-zero-app
bun install
bun run dev
```

Legacy wrapper:

```sh
./scripts/create-project.sh ../my-zero-app --skip-install
```

The wrapper delegates to `create-zero --local`; it must not copy or directly
link framework source into the app.

## Safe Local Update Workflow

Stop the app/dev server, then refresh an existing checkout-local app without
regenerating it:

```sh
cd /path/to/zero-platform
bun run install:local-tools
cd /path/to/my-zero-app
zero-update --dry-run
zero-update --check
```

The wrapper consumes the package saved from committed local `main` by the
checkout that installed it. It never packs that checkout's live working tree,
does not fall back when the saved archive is missing or corrupt, and manages
only the exact `file:./.zero/framework/zero-framework.tgz` dependency, its
ignored archive cache, the installed framework package, and Bun install state.
Use `zero update --project <app> --local <checkout>` explicitly when testing an
unreleased working checkout. The app must have exactly one committed `bun.lock`
or `bun.lockb`, including for a dry-run. A clean clone may omit `.zero/`,
`.zero/framework/`, the archive, and `node_modules`; a mutating update creates
the managed cache and installs Zero, while `--dry-run` reports the pending
bootstrap without creating anything. Existing symlinks or wrong-type managed
entries are rejected.

The default update does not rewrite app source, configuration, environment
files, databases, or storage and runs no app-defined scripts. `--check` runs
the app's existing typecheck and Doctor scripts, whose side effects are outside
updater rollback. Zero never selects or runs migrations. Never use
`create-zero --force` or `zero-new --force` as an updater.

## Generated App Shape

`create-zero` generates app-owned files only:

```txt
app/
  layout.tsx
  page.tsx
  server.ts
server/
  endpoints/
  middleware/
  plugins/
  resources/
  routes/
components/
hooks/
lib/
db/
  schema.ts
zero.config.ts
.env.example
.gitignore
package.json
README.md
tsconfig.json
```

Generated build glue lives in `.zero/generated` and is ignored by git.
Framework runtime stays in `node_modules/@zero/framework`.

The generated TypeScript aliases resolve app-owned `components/`, `hooks/`,
and `lib/` files first, then fall back to the installed framework source for
Zero's internal aliases. App code must still use public `@zero/framework/*`
imports instead of reaching into `node_modules` directly.

Generated starter `app/layout.tsx` and `app/page.tsx` are server-rendered by
default. The first public page should ship HTML content and the platform
stylesheet without client route JavaScript. Add a top-level `"use client"`
directive only to pages or layouts that need browser hooks, AppShell
interactivity, ReactiveDB hooks, forms, or other client-side behavior.

## Canonical Imports

Backend startup and server extensions:

```ts
import {
  createApp,
  defineEndpoint,
  defineMiddleware,
  defineResource,
  defineRouter,
  defineZeroConfig,
} from '@zero/framework/server';
```

Schema:

```ts
import { defineTable, field } from '@zero/framework/schema';
```

Frontend providers and hooks:

```tsx
import { AppProvider } from '@zero/framework/react/app-provider';
import {
  useAuth,
  useCollection,
  useLazyCollection,
  useResourceList,
} from '@zero/framework/react/hooks';
```

UI:

```tsx
import { AppShell } from '@zero/framework/components/app-shell';
import { Button } from '@zero/framework/components/ui/button';
import { DataTableView } from '@zero/framework/components/data-table';
import { MasterDetailView } from '@zero/framework/components/master-detail';
import { KanbanBoard } from '@zero/framework/components/kanban';
```

Icons:

```tsx
import { AnimateIcon, Check, Trash, ZeroIcon } from '@zero/framework/icons';
```

Subsystem imports exist for advanced use:

- `@zero/framework/auth`
- `@zero/framework/email`
- `@zero/framework/kv`
- `@zero/framework/migrations`
- `@zero/framework/notifications`
- `@zero/framework/observability`
- `@zero/framework/pdf`
- `@zero/framework/persistence`
- `@zero/framework/resources`
- `@zero/framework/rooms`
- `@zero/framework/scheduler`
- `@zero/framework/storage`
- `@zero/framework/sync`
- `@zero/framework/sync/client`
- `@zero/framework/tokens`
- `@zero/framework/vector`
- `@zero/framework/workflows`

Use narrow frontend imports in package-mode apps. The broad
`@zero/framework/react` barrel is available, but it exposes a large surface.

## Composition Root

`zero.config.ts` owns runtime settings:

```ts
import { defineZeroConfig } from '@zero/framework/server';
import { tables } from './db/schema';

const PORT = Number(Bun.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const hasEmail = Boolean(Bun.env.RESEND_API_KEY);
const hasAI = Boolean(
  Bun.env.OPENAI_API_KEY ||
    Bun.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ||
    Bun.env.GEMINI_API_KEY ||
    Bun.env.GOOGLE_API_KEY ||
    Bun.env.GROQ_API_KEY ||
    Bun.env.LLAMA_API_KEY ||
    Bun.env.META_LLAMA_API_KEY
);
const hasPdf = Bun.env.ZERO_PDF_ENABLED === 'true';

const config = defineZeroConfig({
  app: {
    name: Bun.env.APP_NAME ?? 'Zero App',
    publicUrl: Bun.env.APP_PUBLIC_URL ?? `http://localhost:${PORT}`,
    supportEmail: Bun.env.APP_SUPPORT_EMAIL,
  },
  db: {
    mode: Bun.env.DB_MODE === 'file'
      ? 'file'
      : Bun.env.DB_MODE === 'ephemeral'
        ? 'ephemeral'
        : 'hot',
    path: Bun.env.DB_PATH ?? './data/app.db',
    snapshotPath: Bun.env.DB_SNAPSHOT_PATH ?? './data/app.snapshot.db',
  },
  tables,
  auth: true,
  routeAuth: 'explicit',
  email: hasEmail
    ? {
        provider: 'resend',
        from: Bun.env.EMAIL_FROM ?? 'Zero App <noreply@example.com>',
        replyTo: Bun.env.EMAIL_REPLY_TO,
        resend: { apiKey: Bun.env.RESEND_API_KEY },
      }
    : false,
  ai: hasAI ? true : false,
  vector: Bun.env.ZERO_VECTOR_ENABLED === 'true'
    ? {
        dataDir: Bun.env.ZERO_VECTOR_DATA_DIR ?? './data/vector',
        defaultDimensions: Number(Bun.env.ZERO_VECTOR_DEFAULT_DIMENSIONS ?? 1536),
      }
    : false,
  pdf: hasPdf
    ? {
        browser: {
          executablePath: Bun.env.ZERO_PDF_EXECUTABLE_PATH,
        },
      }
    : false,
  stateSync: true,
  sitemap: {
    enabled: true,
    changefreq: 'weekly',
    priority: 0.7,
    exclude: ['/login', '/forgot-password', '/reset-password'],
  },
  appDir: './app',
  serverPluginsDir: './server/plugins',
  serverMiddlewareDir: './server/middleware',
  serverEndpointsDir: './server/endpoints',
  serverRoutesDir: './server/routes',
  generatedDir: './.zero/generated',
  outDir: './.build',
  port: PORT,
});

export default config;
export { config };
```

`app/server.ts` should stay small:

```ts
import { createApp } from '@zero/framework/server';
import config from '../zero.config';

const app = await createApp(config);
app.listen(config.port ?? 3000);
```

## Runtime Systems Mounted By createApp

`createApp()` currently installs these systems when configured:

| System | Runtime behavior |
| --- | --- |
| ReactiveDB | App tables from `tables`; server writes emit sync changes. |
| ReactiveDB Fabric | With `databaseTopology`, actor-owned application databases use validated file/WAL, bounded hot, or hybrid placement while the control/auth database stays pinned. |
| Shared SQL | Platform SQLite service available as `zero.sql`/`zero.sqlite`. |
| WebSocket sync | Mounted at `/sync`; auth and resource-policy aware. |
| `/api/data` | Lazy table query API with pagination, sorting, filters, limits, and policy integration. |
| Auth | `/auth/*`, account lifecycle, tokens, session helpers, route auth. |
| Email | Resend default or custom provider boundary. |
| Storage | Local drives, object routes, permissions, uploads, public upload grants. |
| KV/cache | Durable memory-first KV, counters, limiters. |
| State sync | Persisted reactive state isolated per authorized-scope user. |
| Notifications | Notifications and per-user receipts when auth is enabled. |
| Rooms/presence | Room membership and presence primitives when auth is enabled. |
| Workflows | Workflow registry/service when auth is enabled. |
| Scheduler | Platform jobs. |
| AI | Server-side AI provider registry/service when enabled. |
| Vector | zvec-backed vector store when enabled. |
| PDF | Lazy browser-grade PDF service when enabled; no public routes. |
| Observability | Stable event codes, sinks, memory store, protected event route. |
| Migrations | CLI/runtime migration support. |
| Sitemap | `/sitemap.xml` from public static file-router pages when enabled. |
| App extensions | Loads `server/plugins`, `server/middleware`, `server/endpoints`, `server/routes`. |
| File router | Handles `app/**/page.tsx`, `layout.tsx`, `route.ts`, 404s. |

## Backend Service Context

App-owned backend handlers receive a lazy `zero` service context. Prefer
canonical names:

- `zero.db`: ReactiveDB writes with sync/change tracking
- `zero.sql` / `zero.sqlite`: direct backend SQL for reporting/internal tables
- `zero.kv`: durable KV/cache
- `zero.counter`: counter helper
- `zero.limiter`: rate limiter helper
- `zero.auth`: auth helpers
- `zero.email`: email service
- `zero.storage`: grouped storage APIs
- `zero.notifications`: notification service
- `zero.scheduler`: scheduler service
- `zero.workflows`: workflow service
- `zero.ai`: AI service
- `zero.vector`: vector store
- `zero.pdf`: browser-grade PDF rendering and storage composition
- `zero.resources`: resource registry
- `zero.observability`: observability sink/service

Use `zero.db` for app tables that should sync. Use `zero.sql` for backend-only
SQL that does not need ReactiveDB change tracking.

## Data Models And ReactiveDB

Define schemas once in `db/schema.ts` and pass the same `tables` object to
`createApp()` and `AppProvider`.

```ts
import { defineTable, field } from '@zero/framework/schema';

export const customers = defineTable(
  'customers',
  {
    name: field.text({ label: 'Name', required: true, tableVisible: true }),
    owner_id: field.text({ label: 'Owner', tableVisible: false }),
    created_at: field.number({ label: 'Created At', integer: true, tableVisible: true }),
  },
  {
    pk: 'customer_id',
    sync: 'auto',
  }
);

export const tables = { customers };
```

ReactiveDB-managed tables require one sync primary key. Do not use composite
primary keys on synced tables. For relationship tables, keep a single sync
primary key and declare a natural identity:

```ts
export const memberships = defineTable(
  'memberships',
  {
    team_id: field.text({ required: true }),
    user_id: field.text({ required: true }),
    role: field.text({ required: true }),
  },
  {
    pk: 'membership_id',
    identity: ['team_id', 'user_id'],
  }
);
```

Zero generates deterministic ids from natural identity values and creates a
unique identity index.

### ReactiveDB Fabric (unreleased branch)

Fabric coordinates multiple independently reactive SQLite databases without
changing the default single-database contract. Configure it only through the
typed `databaseTopology` surface. Application code receives a database client
already bound from trusted server authority; URL parameters, request bodies,
headers, and browser messages never choose a file or logical database.

In tenant-database mode, tables physically stored per tenant do not need a
`tenant_id` column merely for isolation. Global/control data remains in the
pinned default database, and logical shared-row tenancy continues to use the
existing tenant-column rules. The Resource registry is the source of truth for
which plane owns each exposed table. Resource CRUD, `/api/data`, and Sync all
follow that server-owned topology and retain their policy and field-access
checks.

File/WAL placement gives each active database one FIFO writer actor. Separate
databases can write concurrently when the topology has multiple writer slots;
an optional reader actor permits committed same-file WAL reads while its writer
is busy. Hot placement is bounded and writer-only. Hybrid placement chooses
file or hot synchronously from an opaque, pseudonymous database reference and
pins that choice for the active entry; it is not live promotion or demotion.
The deterministic reference is unkeyed operational correlation metadata, not
a secret or authorization capability, and a low-entropy source ID can be
guess-correlated.

Fabric has independent hard limits for active actor entries, durable database
files, tenant-Sync-pinned databases, per-database Sync bindings, queues,
receipts, and snapshot sessions. Permanent physical or receipt-key exhaustion
uses `DATABASE_CAPACITY_EXHAUSTED`; transient admission pressure uses
`DATABASE_BACKPRESSURE`. Do not catch either and silently bypass the
coordinator. Use Doctor and Zero observability to plan capacity and lifecycle.

Replacement backoff belongs to one database entry. The default
`databaseTopology.restart` policy waits 10 ms initially, caps exponential
delay at 1 second, and uses a 5-second half-open cadence after five attempts.
Waiting operations retain queue timeout/cancellation; the last lease and app
shutdown cancel pending replacement delays.

This is active implementation on an unmerged child branch. Before treating it
as supported, follow the remaining gates in
[ReactiveDB Fabric: Multi-Database Architecture](docs/framework/multi-database-architecture.md).

## Sync Modes

Table sync defaults to `auto`.

- Small tables stay in full WebSocket snapshots.
- Oversized tables auto-resolve to lazy sync.
- Explicit lazy tables skip initial snapshots and load on demand through
  `collection.load()`, `useLazyCollection()`, `/api/data`, DataTable source
  contracts, or MasterDetail source contracts.
- Authorized live changes still stream after rows are present locally.
- Ring-buffer reconnect replays missed changes when possible.
- Same-row optimistic mutations are serialized.
- Disconnected sends are buffered and flushed on reconnect.

Sync mode controls loading, not authorization. For auth-enabled `createApp()`:

- `users`, workflow definitions, and Storage drive/object metadata are private
  from generic Sync snapshots, catch-up, and live delivery;
- notifications and receipts are target/owner scoped;
- rooms and room members require actual membership, including for a global
  administrator;
- workflow execution rows are starter-scoped, with the documented legacy
  global-administrator workflow override;
- framework-owned tables reject direct Sync mutation; use their supported HTTP
  or service APIs; and
- app-owned tables still need an explicit resource/Sync policy appropriate to
  the application's data.

These decisions compose deny-wins with application resource policy. A local
hook filter such as `useQuery()` or `useRoomData()` is only presentation logic;
it cannot replace server read-row and mutation policy. Lower-level standalone
`createSyncPlugin()` intentionally retains public/allow-all compatibility, so
private deployments must configure both WebSocket auth and read/write policy.

## Frontend Root Provider

Root `app/layout.tsx` should usually own providers only:

```tsx
'use client';

import type { ReactNode } from 'react';
import { AppProvider } from '@zero/framework/react/app-provider';
import { ThemeProvider } from '@zero/framework/components/ui/theme-provider';
import { Toaster } from '@zero/framework/components/ui/sonner';
import { tables } from '../db/schema';

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="system" storageKey="zero-theme">
      <AppProvider
        url={typeof window !== 'undefined' ? window.location.origin : ''}
        tables={tables}
      >
        <div className="min-h-screen bg-background text-foreground font-sans antialiased">
          {children}
        </div>
        <Toaster />
      </AppProvider>
    </ThemeProvider>
  );
}
```

Do not force every page into `AppShell` at the root. Put visual shells lower in
the route tree.

## File Router, Layouts, And Auth Boundaries

Use route groups for sibling layouts without changing URLs:

```txt
app/
  layout.tsx
  (public)/
    page.tsx
    intake/resume/[token]/page.tsx
  (dashboard)/
    layout.tsx
    dashboard/page.tsx
```

Public-first app config:

```ts
defineZeroConfig({
  auth: true,
  routeAuth: 'explicit',
  loginPath: '/login',
  postLoginPath: '/dashboard',
});
```

Protected dashboard layout:

```tsx
import { AppShell, type RouteConfig } from '@zero/framework/react';

export const config: RouteConfig = {
  auth: 'required',
};

export default function DashboardLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <AppShell>{children}</AppShell>;
}
```

Internal app config:

```ts
defineZeroConfig({
  auth: true,
  routeAuth: 'protected-by-default',
  publicPaths: ['/login', '/forgot-password', '/verify-email'],
});
```

If a session expires or refresh fails on a protected route, Zero clears
protected UI and redirects to `loginPath` with exactly one validated,
URL-encoded `redirect` return path. A direct server redirect preserves pathname
and query. Client navigation can also preserve the fragment, which is never
sent to the server. Once the configured login route is authenticated, one safe
return path wins; otherwise `postLoginPath` (default `/`) is used with
replacement navigation.

Return paths must be bounded root-relative local URLs. External,
scheme-relative, malformed, duplicate, recursive, backslash/control-character,
and canonicalization-unsafe values are ignored. `/login` and `/login/` are the
same route for loop prevention. An explicit `postLoginPath` resolving to
`loginPath` is rejected. For compatibility, `loginPath: '/'` with the implicit
default `/` post-login path remains a no-op for authenticated root visits.

`postLoginPath` is a top-level `createApp()`/`defineZeroConfig()` option and an
`AppProvider` override, not an `auth` or raw `createClient()` field. Packaged and
custom auth forms keep their success callbacks; inside `AppProvider`, use them
for side effects instead of duplicating normal login navigation.

`useAuth().isRestoring` is true only while a persisted browser session rotates
its refresh token and loads `/auth/me`; `isLoading` is also true. `AppProvider`
withholds the login subtree during that interval. Browsers with Web Locks
serialize rotation per Zero server across tabs and workers and reread the
persisted token after acquiring the lock. Without Web Locks, Zero uses a
bounded, expiring `localStorage` bakery lock across tabs when browser storage
is available. The in-process queue is the final same-JavaScript-realm fallback
for runtimes without either facility.

## Sitemap

Enable sitemap in config:

```ts
sitemap: {
  enabled: true,
  changefreq: 'weekly',
  priority: 0.7,
  exclude: ['/login', '/forgot-password', '/reset-password'],
}
```

Zero serves `/sitemap.xml` from public static file-router pages. It omits API
routes, dynamic routes, protected routes, catch-all routes, and route-group
folder names unless manual entries are configured.

## App-Owned Backend Extensions

Zero loads app-owned backend folders in this order:

| Folder | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `server/plugins/` | Advanced app plugins created with Zero helpers or raw Elysia plugins. |
| `server/middleware/` | Named middleware with path/method/predicate matchers and auth policy. |
| `server/endpoints/` | Single Zero-native endpoints. |
| `server/routes/` | Grouped routers and raw Elysia escape-hatch plugins. |
| `server/resources/` | Resource declarations for generated CRUD and policy integration. |

Example router:

```ts
import { t } from 'elysia';
import { defineEndpoint, defineRouter } from '@zero/framework/server';

export default defineRouter({
  name: 'app.customers',
  prefix: '/api/customers',
  endpoints: [
    defineEndpoint({
      method: 'POST',
      path: '/',
      auth: 'user',
      body: t.Object({
        name: t.String({ minLength: 1 }),
      }),
      handler: ({ body, user, zero }) => {
        return zero.db.insert('customers', {
          customer_id: crypto.randomUUID(),
          name: body.name,
          owner_id: user.userId,
          created_at: Date.now(),
        }).row;
      },
    }),
  ],
});
```

Use Elysia validation (`t.Object`, `t.String`, etc.) for runtime validation and
type inference. Keep route handlers thin.

## Middleware And Policy

Use middleware matchers for cross-cutting server policy. Match by `path`,
`method`, and optional `predicate`. Enforce with `auth`, `role`, and
`properties`.

Property matchers use configured auth user properties. Authorization-grade
properties must be marked trusted in config and must not be self-editable.

Security must live on the server. UI gates can hide buttons, but server policy
must enforce access.

## Resources And Generated CRUD

Use resources when an app table needs server-side CRUD, `/api/data` policy, and
WebSocket sync policy integration.

Every multi-mode resource declares server-owned `exposure`: `internal`,
`http`, `sync`, or `all`. Omission retains legacy `all` only in single mode.
`_sync` and `syncDefaults` choose loading strategy, not authority. A
`sync`-only resource must stay full Sync; lazy or auto-lazy Sync hydration
requires `all` because it also uses `/api/data`. An HTTP-only resource may use
`/api/data` without joining Sync.

Omitting `actions` enables the standard list/get/create/update/delete set.
Explicit `actions: []` enables none. A per-action policy map may name only
declared actions; unknown or extra keys are rejected.

Important helpers:

- `defineResource()`
- `ownerPolicy()`
- `metadataPolicy()`
- `authorizationPolicy()` — the same structured live RBAC requirement used by
  routes, enforced across generated CRUD, `/api/data`, and Sync
- `adminOnly()`
- `anyOf()`
- `allOf()`
- `validateResourcePolicy()`
- `evaluateResourcePolicy()`

Generated routes default to:

- `GET /api/resources/:resource`
- `GET /api/resources/:resource/:id`
- `POST /api/resources/:resource`
- `PATCH /api/resources/:resource/:id`
- `DELETE /api/resources/:resource/:id`

Generated route writes go through ReactiveDB and enforce resource policies
server-side.

`/api/data` enforces registered resource `list` policy for lazy tables.
WebSocket sync enforces resource list/write policy too. Row-constrained list
policies use row-filtered sync.

Keep the enforceable declaration in a server-only resource module next to the
shared schema. `defineTable()` metadata and `sync: 'full' | 'lazy' | 'auto'`
are not access control and must not contain executable client-trusted policy.

## Auth

The current tree keeps the existing global identity/legacy-global-role model
and adds independent tenancy and authorization axes. The legacy `admin` role
does not supply advanced application permissions, and those permissions do not
promote the legacy role:

```ts
auth: {
  tenancy: 'single',
  authorization: 'simple',
}
```

Omitting either field has the same result. All four explicit profiles are
implemented. Multi mode requires classified registered resources and uses
tenant-bound durable sessions; advanced mode expands retained scoped role
assignments through the same kernel. User/session projections come from auth
APIs; generic Sync does not expose the `users` table under default
`createApp()` policy. Raw SQL and deliberate `zero.unsafe` use remain trusted
application code outside Zero's tenant-isolation guarantee.

When `authorization` is an object, its positive `registryVersion` defaults to
`1`. Increment it before deploying any same-profile permission/role semantic
change; labels and descriptions alone do not require a bump. Migration `027`
persists a semantic fingerprint. Same-version drift, rollback, corrupt
markers, and reintroducing a role key while retained live assignments still
name it fail startup. A supported profile-axis transition may keep the version
only when permission, role, and evaluator semantics are otherwise identical;
combined profile-and-registry semantic changes require a bump. Successful
registry changes are system-audited and stale
runtimes fail closed until restarted. The public auth config exposes only the
authorization mode, never this server-only manifest.

Zero auth supports:

- enabled/disabled auth
- secret-gated, durable installation bootstrap by default; explicit public
  first-request compatibility or disabled/trusted provisioning modes
- public registration or admin-only registration
- admin-created users and setup emails
- password reset/setup action tokens
- email verification during account creation
- optional or required MFA
- email OTP MFA
- authenticator/TOTP MFA
- self-hosted TOTP secret encryption
- refresh token rotation
- durable application/tenant session persistence, refresh, selection, and switching
- admin user management
- single/advanced application access management
- protected Administration Organization people/invitation management and
  permission-gated customer-organization lifecycle
- tenant member and role administration
- exact-email invitations, invitation-bound registration, and retained join requests
- sanitized browser authorization snapshots and permission/tenant/platform gates
- configured public/private user properties
- property-based backend policy
- desktop/mobile/extension public clients using the same users and
  authorization policy

In multi mode the browser authorization snapshot keeps the active membership
in tenant `scope`. While the active tenant is the protected Administration
Organization, additive `applicationScope` carries its application permissions.
Permission helpers and `PermissionGate` inspect both projections;
tenant-role/tenant-ID gates inspect only `scope`. The opaque snapshot revision
covers both planes and the installed registry version. These are UI hints,
never server authority.

Common auth config:

```ts
auth: {
  tenancy: 'single',
  authorization: 'simple',
  bootstrap: {
    mode: 'secret',
    secret: Bun.env.AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_SECRET || undefined,
  },
  registration: { mode: 'admin-only' },
  account: {
    requireEmailVerification: Bun.env.AUTH_REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION === 'true',
    emailVerificationPath: '/verify-email',
  },
  mfa: {
    enabled: Bun.env.AUTH_MFA_ENABLED === 'true',
    policy: 'optional',
    methods: ['email', 'totp'],
    allowUserChoice: true,
    allowMultipleMethods: false,
    recoveryCodes: false,
    totp: {
      issuer: Bun.env.APP_NAME ?? 'Zero App',
      encryptionKey: Bun.env.AUTH_TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY,
    },
  },
  accountEmails: {
    adminCreatedUser: true,
    passwordReset: true,
    manualPasswordReset: Bun.env.AUTH_MANUAL_PASSWORD_RESET !== 'false',
    actionTokenTTL: '1h',
    requestCooldown: '5m',
  },
}
```

Auth UI components:

- `AuthLayout`
- `LoginForm`
- `RegisterForm`
- `ForgotPasswordForm`
- `EmailVerificationForm`
- `PasswordActionForm`
- `ChangePasswordForm`
- `PasswordInput`
- `PasswordStrength`
- `OTPVerification`
- `MFAContinuation`
- `MFAEnrollmentForm`
- `MFAChallengeForm`
- `MFAManagementPanel`
- `AuthFlowContinuation`
- `TenantSelectionForm`
- `TenantCreationForm`
- `TenantSwitcher`
- `TenantMemberManagement`
- `TenantInvitationForm`
- `TenantOnboardingManagement`
- `ApplicationAccessManagement`
- `PlatformAdministrationManagement`
- `PlatformTenantManagement`
- `PermissionGate`
- `TenantGate`
- `PlatformAdminGate`
- `UserPropertiesForm`
- `SignedIn`
- `SignedOut`
- `AdminGate`
- property gates

Use these instead of building custom auth forms unless the app has a strong
reason.

### Installed app auth

Choose the surface before implementing a host bridge:

- `@zero/framework/native` is the implemented TypeScript native core in the
  current source. Pin a published framework release that includes the export;
  source presence alone is not proof that an older package version has it.
- `zero-native-auth` and `tauri-plugin-zero-auth` are standalone Rust/Tauri
  `0.0.0` private previews with OIDC discovery, Authorization Code + PKCE,
  callback/state validation, rotating sessions, tenant operations,
  authenticated HTTP, vault adapters, and Tauri commands. They still require
  independent release ownership, versioning, license, platform adapter, and
  security gates.
- `@zero/chrome-auth` is a standalone private `0.0.0` Chrome MV3 preview. It
  has no released framework peer range, real-Chrome release gate, or
  independent security review yet. Do not treat it as an installable registry
  package.

All installed apps use the system browser and Authorization Code + PKCE. They
reuse Zero accounts, registration, verification, recovery, MFA, roles, trusted
properties, endpoint/middleware auth, resources, live revocation, and Sync
policy. OIDC scopes release identity claims only; they are not application
permissions. Native apps never receive a client secret, API key, signing key,
or manually configured public key.

Register one publishable client ID per independently shipped app:

```ts
app: {
  name: 'Acme',
  publicUrl: 'https://app.acme.example',
},
auth: {
  nativeApps: {
    clients: [{
      clientId: 'acme-desktop',
      name: 'Acme Desktop',
      redirectUris: [
        'http://127.0.0.1/oauth/callback',
        'http://[::1]/oauth/callback',
      ],
      scopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email'],
    }],
  },
}
```

`app.publicUrl` is a canonical HTTPS origin outside exact loopback
development. The OIDC issuer is that origin plus `/auth`; the access JWT
audience is the exact app origin and the ID-token audience is the public client
ID. A separate issuer/API origin is unsupported. The current discovery document
has no Zero profile-version extension, so third-party clients must validate
advertised capabilities and pin a tested framework release.

Supported redirects are claimed HTTPS, reverse-domain single-slash private
schemes, and IP-literal HTTP loopback. Only a loopback port may differ from the
registered URI. Chrome uses the exact stable
`https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/zero-auth/callback` returned by
`chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`.

Create the preferred TypeScript owner in a trusted JavaScript process:

```ts
import {
  createNativeSyncAuth,
  createZeroNativeAuthBroker,
} from '@zero/framework/native';
import { createSyncClient } from '@zero/framework/sync/client';

const auth = createZeroNativeAuthBroker({
  serverUrl: 'https://app.acme.example',
  clientId: 'acme-desktop',
  browser: systemBrowser,
  callback: callbackAdapter,
  secureStorage: osSecureVault,
});

await auth.initialize();
await auth.signIn();
const response = await auth.fetch('/api/account');

const syncAuth = createNativeSyncAuth(auth);
const sync = createSyncClient({
  url: 'wss://app.acme.example/sync',
  tables,
  ...syncAuth,
});
```

Use an OS keychain/keystore, never renderer storage or a normal file. Keep one
broker per process/vault namespace. Electron renderers use the revision-ordered
broker proxy over narrow IPC. A Rust-first Tauri main process cannot host the
TypeScript broker, and the broker must not be moved into a Svelte webview; wait
for the Rust SDK or use a separately threat-modeled trusted JavaScript sidecar
for a prototype.

Spread the entire Sync adapter. Its lifecycle binder prevents anonymous cold
start, refreshes after auth closes, purges cached rows/pending mutations on
sign-out or account change, and reconnects only for an authenticated subject.

Mobile runtimes must provide standards-compatible global WebCrypto
(`getRandomValues` and `subtle`), `fetch`, `URL`, and `TextEncoder`. Expo/React
Native compatibility is not assumed. The Chrome preview uses one module-scope
service-worker owner and a fixed token-free UI message protocol. Privileged
extension pages remain trusted because Chrome storage is not worker-isolated;
session mode targets Chrome 116+ and opt-in local persistence Chrome 140+.

Source admission is safe by default: direct deployments use Bun's socket peer
and ignore forwarded headers. Behind a proxy, configure only exact trusted
proxy address/CIDR ranges. Do not add a custom `sourceKey` merely because
client IDs are public; it is for a deployment with a trustworthy non-IP edge
identity. Multi-process deployments still need shared edge limits; local
process-pseudonymous admission identities must not be treated as a global edge
limit.

Run `bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --strict`, review the normal
database migration/backup path, and test browser registration, verification,
MFA/recovery, callback/cold launch, rotation, revocation, protected HTTP, Sync
cache purge, and account switching on real targets. Read
`docs/auth/app-auth-sdk-guide.md`, `docs/auth/native-app-auth.md`, and
`examples/native-auth/README.md` before implementation.

## Email

Zero email uses a provider boundary. Resend is the default provider when
configured:

```ts
email: {
  provider: 'resend',
  from: Bun.env.EMAIL_FROM ?? 'Zero App <noreply@example.com>',
  replyTo: Bun.env.EMAIL_REPLY_TO,
  resend: { apiKey: Bun.env.RESEND_API_KEY },
}
```

Auth/account emails use branded defaults from app config. User apps can replace
provider behavior through custom provider/adapters. Keep auth email templates
themeable and app-name aware.

## Platform Tokens

Platform tokens support one-time action tokens and resumable public-flow
tokens. Use them for:

- password reset/setup
- email verification
- public intake resume links
- upload grants
- one-time app actions

Token validation should happen server-side. Resume tokens can point to draft
records or form state records, but the token service should remain generic.

Auth password/account actions layer `AuthActionTokenService` over the generic
platform service. Both stores must use the exact same `ReactiveDB` instance,
not merely the same file path or database configuration. `createApp()` mounts
platform tokens before auth and injects the correct app-local service
automatically. Direct plugin composition must pass that same service through
`platformTokenService` or `getPlatformTokenService`; a mismatched transaction
domain fails closed with `AUTH_STATE_INVARIANT_FAILED`.

Action-token consumption joins the outer auth transaction. Platform and auth
consumed-success observability is queued after the outermost commit, so a
credential/account rollback preserves the token and emits no false success.
Read `docs/tokens.md#auth-transaction-boundary` before directly composing the
two plugins.

## Storage

Zero storage provides:

- local drives/buckets
- object routes
- object metadata
- drive and object permissions
- public upload grants
- scoped upload tokens
- presigned/private download flows
- storage hooks
- storage management UI

Use `zero.storage` server-side. Storage APIs are grouped:

- `storage.drives`
- `storage.objects`
- `storage.permissions`
- `storage.uploads`

Frontend components:

- `StorageManagement`
- `StorageDriveList`
- `StorageDriveDetail`
- `StorageDriveSettingsPanel`
- `StorageDrivePermissionsPanel`
- `StorageDropzone`
- `StorageFileBrowser`
- `StorageDriveDetailHeader`
- `StorageFileDetailPanel`

Frontend hooks:

- `useUpload`
- `useUploadQueue`
- `useUploadDropzone`
- `useStorageFile`
- `useStorageBrowser`
- `useStorageDrives`
- `useDriveCapabilities`
- `useStoragePermissions`
- `useDriveQuota`

Use the storage organism for admin/storage tooling before writing bespoke UI.

## KV And Persistence

Zero persistence supports:

- `hot`: memory-first active SQLite with snapshot recovery
- `file`: direct SQLite/WAL mode
- `ephemeral`: tests/in-memory use

Zero KV/cache is memory-first with journal/checkpoint recovery. It supports:

- namespaced keys
- TTL
- LRU bounds
- counters
- rate limiters
- `getOrSet`

Generated apps normally use `zero.kv`, `zero.counter`, and `zero.limiter`
inside backend routes instead of importing the KV engine directly.

## State Sync, Rooms, Presence, Notifications

State sync:

- per-authorized-scope user server-persisted reactive key/value state
- useful for preferences and UI state

Hooks:

- `useServerState`
- `usePreference`
- `useFormDraft`

Rooms/presence:

- membership-scoped built-in `rooms` and `room_members` rows
- online/idle/away presence
- typing indicators
- ephemeral topics

The room HTTP `join` action does not admit an arbitrary authenticated user. It
is idempotent only for a user already admitted by trusted server-side app
policy. Room detail and member lists require actual membership; global admin is
not a data-plane read bypass. A room owner cannot leave and orphan the room;
the route returns `409 ROOM_OWNER_CANNOT_LEAVE`. Global-admin room deletion is
a separate control-plane compatibility rule.

App-owned rows with a `room_id` are not protected automatically.
`useRoomData(roomId, table)` is a client-side filter, so the app must enforce
membership and validate or stamp `room_id` in server read/write policy.
Presence, typing, and other ephemeral helpers currently use caller-selected
topic names. A `presence:${roomId}` topic does not prove membership; keep those
payloads non-sensitive until server-derived topic authorization exists.

Hooks:

- `usePresence`
- `usePresenceList`
- `useTypingIndicator`
- `useEphemeral`
- `useEphemeralTopic`

Notifications:

- targeted notifications
- receipts
- read/dismiss actions
- sync-backed UI updates

Default `createApp()` projects notification rows only to actual targets and
receipt rows only to their owning user. The protected administrator receipt
audit is an HTTP view, not a generic all-receipts Sync subscription.

Hooks:

- `useNotifications`
- `useUnreadCount`

## Workflows And Scheduler

Zero workflows and scheduler are in-process platform services. Use them for
app-owned background orchestration, scheduled work, and domain workflows.

Workflow definitions are authenticated shared metadata over the purpose-built
HTTP API, not generic Sync rows. Normal instance lists and instance/step/event
reads are starter-scoped; send/cancel/pause/resume use the same owner check,
with the documented legacy global-administrator workflow authority. Missing and
inaccessible instance IDs both return 404.

Hooks:

- `useWorkflowRun`
- `useWorkflow`
- `useWorkflowList`

Server services:

- `zero.workflows`
- `zero.scheduler`

Future extension points include workflow-trigger webhooks and AI tools that
can invoke workflows, but do not invent those unless they exist in the current
framework.

## AI

Zero AI is internal/server-side by default. It is not a public gateway unless
an app deliberately builds that.

Provider keys enable providers at runtime:

- `OPENAI_API_KEY`
- `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
- `GEMINI_API_KEY` / `GOOGLE_API_KEY`
- `GROQ_API_KEY`
- `XAI_API_KEY`
- `COHERE_API_KEY`
- `LLAMA_API_KEY` / `META_LLAMA_API_KEY`
- `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`
- `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY`
- `VOYAGE_API_KEY`
- `DEEPGRAM_API_KEY`

Aliases:

- `ZERO_AI_FAST_MODEL`
- `ZERO_AI_SMART_MODEL`
- `ZERO_AI_EMBEDDING_MODEL`
- `ZERO_AI_IMAGE_MODEL`
- `ZERO_AI_TRANSCRIPTION_MODEL`
- `ZERO_AI_SPEECH_MODEL`

Use `zero.ai` from backend routes. The AI layer supports:

- text generation
- structured output through the underlying AI SDK where configured
- embeddings
- image generation
- transcription
- speech
- conversation helpers
- tool helpers
- workflow bridge helpers
- provider status/readiness

Do not expose provider keys to the frontend.

## Vector Store

Zero vector storage is zvec-backed and local. It provides:

- collections
- upserts
- search/query
- metadata filters/scopes
- AI embedding bridge helpers

Enable with:

```ts
vector: {
  dataDir: Bun.env.ZERO_VECTOR_DATA_DIR ?? './data/vector',
  defaultDimensions: Number(Bun.env.ZERO_VECTOR_DEFAULT_DIMENSIONS ?? 1536),
}
```

Use `zero.vector` server-side. Zero does not need to provide native embedding
or reranking for every use case; pair vector storage with the AI embedding
service when needed.

## PDF Rendering

Zero PDF is internal server infrastructure, not a public gateway. Enable it in
`zero.config.ts`, then install the Playwright Chromium revision once per
development machine or production image:

```sh
bun run pdf:install
bun run pdf:status
```

Use the canonical server service:

```ts
if (!zero.pdf) throw new Error('PDF rendering is disabled.');

const rendered = await zero.pdf.render({
  html: '<main><h1>Patient intake</h1></main>',
  css: `
    @page { size: Letter; margin: 0.5in; }
    body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  `,
  document: { title: 'Patient intake', lang: 'en' },
});

return new Response(rendered.bytes, {
  headers: { 'content-type': rendered.contentType },
});
```

Use `zero.pdf.renderToStorage(input, target)` when the generated PDF should be
written through Zero storage. It returns render metadata plus the canonical
storage object. Prefer returning object IDs/paths from workflow steps rather
than putting raw PDF bytes in durable workflow state.

The default Chromium adapter supports modern browser layout, web fonts,
`@media print`, `@page`, backgrounds, page breaks, header/footer templates,
and tagged output. Secure defaults disable JavaScript, service workers, and
downloads; deny remote HTTP(S), `file:`, and private-network resources; and
enforce HTML/CSS/output byte limits, timeout, concurrency, and queue limits.
Allow trusted remote assets by exact origin only.

Zero mounts no PDF endpoint. App-owned endpoints own auth, validation, record
policy, and response behavior. Do not recreate the old Python PDF microservice
or expose raw renderer options. For direct adapter/types access use
`@zero/framework/pdf`. See `docs/pdf.md`.

## Migrations

Zero migrations provide:

- explicit migration files
- migration ledger
- schema history
- drift inspection
- draft migration plans
- rollback safety classification
- backups for destructive changes
- doctor integration

Useful commands:

```sh
bun run migrate:status
bun run migrate:plan
bun run migrate:doctor
zero migrate --doctor --schema ./db/schema.ts --strict
```

Do not rely on ad hoc database mutations for app schema changes when migration
tooling applies.

## Observability

Zero observability provides:

- stable event codes
- default console sink
- bounded memory event store
- protected event endpoint
- frontend event ingest
- app/provider sink boundary

New logs, warnings, caught errors, and lifecycle events should flow through the
observability boundary. Use stable codes/prefixes rather than random console
messages in reusable framework code.

## Platform Doctor

Run doctor against config:

```sh
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --strict
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --json
zero-doctor --config ./zero.config.ts
```

Doctor checks include:

- app config
- primary keys and natural identities
- auth/email readiness
- login/public route safety
- storage/auth mismatch
- migration startup policy
- sync policy/index guidance
- observability endpoint readiness
- AI provider/alias readiness
- vector index/storage safety
- PDF browser path, remote resource policy, private-network access, and
  JavaScript safety
- resource policy shape
- `/api/data` and WebSocket policy implications
- source usage audit warnings when app code bypasses Zero UI primitives,
  modal/toast/sidebar systems, icons, data/sync hooks, backend service
  boundaries, observability, root providers, or public package imports
- large app-owned source files above the responsibility threshold, default 400
  lines

Use `--strict` in CI.

Useful usage-audit switches:

```sh
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --no-usage-audit
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --max-file-lines 400
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --usage-include app --usage-include server
bun run doctor -- --config ./zero.config.ts --usage-exclude app/vendor/**
```

If an app creates non-unique indexes through migrations or narrow startup
compatibility code, declare them in config so Doctor can suppress false index
guidance while still checking real gaps:

```ts
doctor: {
  indexedFields: {
    tickets: ['owner_id'],
  },
}
```

This is only a Doctor hint. The app must still create the real SQLite index.

Agent rule: after generating or editing an app, run doctor and fix usage
warnings before inventing custom components, services, or framework wiring.

## Frontend Hook Library

Platform hooks:

| Area | Hooks |
| --- | --- |
| Auth/session and access | `useAuth`, `useAuthConfig`, `useCurrentUser`, `useRequireAuth`, `useUserProperty`, `useAuthorization`, `useAuthorizationScopeBoundary`, `useHasPermission`, `useHasAllPermissions`, `useHasAnyPermission`, `useApplicationAccess`, `usePlatformAdministration`, `usePlatformTenants`, `useAuthAudit`, `useTenantMembers`, `useTenantOnboardingAdministration`, `useTenantDomainAdministration`, `useDomainOnboarding`, `useTenantSwitcher` |
| Live data | `useCollection`, `useLazyCollection`, `useDataPage`, `useRecord`, `useRecordByIdentity`, `useDataSelection` |
| Resources | `useResourceClient`, `useResourceList`, `useResourceRecord`, `useResourceActions` |
| Storage | `useUpload`, `useUploadQueue`, `useUploadDropzone`, `useStorageFile`, `useStorageBrowser`, `useStorageDrives`, `useDriveCapabilities`, `useStoragePermissions`, `useDriveQuota` |
| Rooms/presence | `usePresence`, `usePresenceList`, `useTypingIndicator`, `useEphemeral`, `useEphemeralTopic` |
| Workflows/notifications | `useWorkflowRun`, `useWorkflow`, `useWorkflowList`, `useNotifications`, `useUnreadCount` |
| State and health | `useServerState`, `usePreference`, `useFormDraft`, `useConnectionHealth`, `useMutation` |

Zero-owned browser hooks fence cached work at the current account/tenant
authorization boundary. App-owned caches must key or purge on the opaque,
credential-free `useAuthorizationScopeBoundary().key`, reject older callbacks,
and hide or freeze scope-sensitive UI while `ready` is false. This key is cache
metadata, never server authority or a substitute for route/resource policy.

Public auth configuration has two intentional caller contracts on one shared,
client-scoped controller. `useAuthConfig().reload()` is nonthrowing and reports
failure through the reactive `status`/`error` snapshot. Imperative
`useAuth().getConfig()` publishes the same safe state but rejects the original
current transport, server, or response-validation failure; a superseded
imperative refresh rejects with `AbortError`. Do not wrap the imperative action
as a nullable failure or bypass the controller with a separate request.

For custom Administration Organization UI, treat
`usePlatformAdministration()` as independent protected-config, member, and
invitation slices. Prefer `isLoadingConfig`/`configError`/`reloadConfig()`,
`isLoadingMembers`/`membersError`/`reloadMembers()`, and
`isLoadingInvitations`/`invitationsError`/`reloadInvitations()` over the
compatibility aggregate fields. Public invitation policy is separately
explicit through `invitationPolicyStatus`, nullable `invitationsEnabled`,
`invitationDelivery`, and `invitationConfigError`.

`useTenantOnboardingAdministration()` likewise has independent protected
config, invitation, and join-request slices. Protected config always loads for
an enabled stable tenant scope and exposes `isLoadingConfig`,
`isConfigPermissionDenied`, `configError`, and `reloadConfig()`, even when both
public features are disabled. Use each feature's own loading, loading-more,
mutation, permission-denied, error, and retry fields. `authConfigStatus`,
`authConfigError`, and the nullable `invitationsEnabled`/
`joinRequestsEnabled` fields describe the separate public-policy prerequisite.
The aggregate fields remain only for backward compatibility; these hooks do
not perform one aggregate list request.

Generic hooks:

- `useAsyncAction`
- `useClickAway`
- `useCopyToClipboard`
- `useDebouncedCallback`
- `useDebouncedValue`
- `useDisclosure`
- `useHotkey`
- `useIdle`
- `useInterval`
- `useMediaQuery`
- `useMounted`
- `useOs`
- `usePrevious`
- `useStableCallback`
- `useTextSelection`
- `useThrottledCallback`
- `useThrottledValue`
- `useTimeout`
- `StickToBottom`
- `useStickToBottom`
- `useStickToBottomContext`

Use these before adding new generic hooks.

## UI Design System Rules

- Use Zero components and tokens.
- Use `AppShell` for dashboards/admin/data apps.
- Use `ResizableNavbar` for public landing/docs/content navigation.
- Use `Hero` for public opening sections.
- Use `TextGenerateEffect`, `TypewriterEffect`, and `FlipWords` for public
  text motion.
- Use `FeaturesSection`, `CodeBlock`, `CtaSection`, `FooterSection`, `Faq`,
  `ExpandableCards`, `BentoGrid`, and `AnimatedList` for common public
  sections.
- Use base `ui/` primitives instead of raw HTML controls.
- Use Zero `Select`, not native `<select>`, in shared/platform UI.
- Use Animate UI/Radix wrappers for overlays, menus, tooltips, dialogs, and
  collapsibles.
- Use Zero animated icons by default.
- Do not use emojis as app action/status icons.
- Check light and dark modes.
- Avoid nested cards.
- Keep UI text inside its container on mobile and desktop.
- Public pages should use the public token lane:
  `public-background`, `public-surface`, `public-glass`, `public-accent`,
  `public-border`, `public-ring`.
- Wrap public route trees with `zero-public-page` or
  `data-zero-page="public"` when using public lane components.

## AppShell Guidance

Use `AppShell` for dashboards:

- workspace switcher
- nested/expandable nav
- sidebar action menus
- footer user menu
- optional breadcrumbs/header row
- optional theme toggle
- custom header content when breadcrumbs are not needed

Use route-group layouts to apply the shell only to dashboard/private branches.
Do not build a one-off sidebar unless `AppShell` cannot express the needed UI.

## DataTable And MasterDetail

Use `DataTableView` and `MasterDetailView` for data-heavy views.

Both should be able to consume app data from:

- in-memory array data
- schema/collection data
- lazy `/api/data` source contracts

Use lazy data for large tables. Use filters/sorting/pagination contracts
instead of custom ad hoc fetch code.

## Kanban

Use `KanbanBoard` for work queues and status boards. Persist actual app state
through ReactiveDB/resources, not local-only UI state. Use the board as a UI
organism and keep domain ownership in app data tables.

## Modal Manager

Use Zero's modal manager for app modals. Do not create a one-off modal stack.
If a modal reopens or loops, fix the modal state integration rather than
forking a new manager.

## Icons

Zero's default icon pack is the Animate UI animated Lucide set.

Use:

```tsx
import { AnimateIcon, Check, Trash, ZeroIcon } from '@zero/framework/icons';
```

`Button` automatically animates nested Zero icons on hover/tap. Outside
`Button`, set `animate`, `animateOnHover`, `animateOnTap`, or wrap with
`AnimateIcon`.

Use `lucide-react` directly only when Zero does not provide the icon.

## zero add

Use packaged imports first. Copy source only when the app needs to customize:

```sh
zero add components/ui/button
zero add components/data-table
zero add components/kanban
zero add components/navbar
zero add components/hero
zero add components/text-effects
zero add hooks modals --dry-run
```

`zero add` skips existing files unless `--force` is provided and rewrites
framework-internal imports to public `@zero/framework/*` paths.

## Package And Distribution

Current package mode is Bun-first:

- package exports point at TypeScript source under `src/`
- CLI bins point at TypeScript source under `src/`
- `create-zero` reads `examples/package-mode`
- package `files` must include `src`, `examples/package-mode`,
  `examples/native-auth`, `docs`,
  `README.md`, `llm.txt`, `llms.txt`, and `CHANGELOG.md`

Run:

```sh
bun run test:package
```

This verifies create-zero, package exports, package scripts, and packed tarball
contents, including outside-tree native SDK resolution and desktop/mobile
recipe compilation.

## Verification

For most code changes:

```sh
bun run typecheck
bun run test:package
bun run build
```

For broad platform changes:

```sh
bun run test
git diff --check
```

Run focused subsystem tests for the touched code. Do not skip tests because the
change is “just docs” if docs change package commands, generated output, or
public API guidance.

## Agent Build Checklist

Before planning an app:

1. Read this file.
2. Identify app shape: public-first, internal-only, or mixed.
3. Decide route auth mode.
4. Define data models in `db/schema.ts`.
5. Use resources/policies for protected CRUD.
6. Use AppShell for dashboards.
7. Use public components for landing/content pages.
8. Use Zero auth/storage/admin/data components before custom UI.
9. Use Zero hooks before new hooks.
10. Use backend `zero` service context before opening direct services manually.
11. Run package/type/build checks after framework changes.

Before creating custom code, ask:

- Does Zero already provide this component?
- Does Zero already provide this hook?
- Does Zero already provide this backend service?
- Does this need server-side policy?
- Does this data need ReactiveDB sync or backend-only SQL?
- Does this document need `zero.pdf.render()` or `renderToStorage()`?
- Does this need a migration?
- Does this need observability?
- Does this affect docs?

## Complete Documentation Catalog

Use this catalog to decide which deeper docs to read. Some files are current
reference docs; others are plans or audits. When a file name includes `plan`,
`audit`, or `roadmap`, treat it as design/history unless the code and current
reference docs confirm the behavior is implemented.

  platform architecture, ReactiveDB, sync, auth, state sync, rooms, presence,

  runtime architecture, frontend/server boundaries, and where to edit.

  hooks, components, icons, storage, auth, and app-facing package exports.
- [Platform Configuration](docs/platform-configuration.md): current explicit
  `AppConfig`/`zero.config.ts` composition for app identity, database modes,
  auth, email, AI, vector, PDF, storage, sync, sitemap, and generated defaults,
  with automatic focused-config discovery labeled as a future proposal.
- [Engineering Standards](docs/engineering-standards.md): repository coding
  standards, Elysia practices, separation of concerns, comments, docs, tests,
  and observability requirements.

  follows Elysia plugin/controller/service/model/lifecycle best practices.

  SQLite behavior, WAL, statements, transactions, and performance choices.
- [Build Plan](docs/build-plan.md): historical/roadmap build plan for earlier
  platform work; verify against current implementation before relying on it.
- [Bootstrap Prompt](docs/bootstrap-prompt.md): prompt text for orienting a new
  assistant on the codebase.
- [Platform Roadmap](docs/platform-roadmap.md): product/build roadmap and future
  platform ideas.
- [Platform Hardening Plan](docs/platform-hardening-plan.md): historical
  hardening plan for backend, frontend, docs, performance, and security.
- [Stabilization Plan](docs/stabilization-plan.md): historical package-mode
  stabilization snapshot; use Releasing Zero for current release gates.
- [Doctor Usage Audit Plan](docs/doctor-usage-audit-plan.md): planned doctor
  source scanner for frontend/backend usage warnings when app code bypasses
  Zero APIs, components, services, or package-mode conventions.
- [Releasing Zero](docs/releasing.md): version bump, verification, package state,
  release checklist, git/tag steps, and package-mode release checks.

  internal AI provider layer, provider registry, aliases, tools, and workflow
  integration.
- [Vector Store](docs/vector.md): zvec-backed vector persistence, collections,
  metadata/scopes, search, upsert, AI embedding bridge, config, and examples.

### Data, Sync, KV, Persistence, And Tokens

- [State Sync](docs/state-sync.md): per-authorized-scope user persistent state sync, client hooks,
  backend routes, optimistic writes, limits, and use cases such as preferences.
- [Platform KV/cache](docs/kv.md): durable memory-first KV/cache service,
  checkpoint/journal recovery, counters, namespaces, TTL, LRU, limiters, and
  `zero.kv` usage.
- [Platform Tokens](docs/tokens.md): generic one-time/resumable token service,
  action tokens, resume tokens, validation, use cases, and security rules.
- [Migrations](docs/migrations.md): migration files, ledger, schema history,
  rollback safety, backups, drift detection, draft planning, and CLI commands.
- [Real-Time Sync Engine](docs/realtime-sync/realtime-sync/README.md): deep
  reference for sync engine architecture, goals, client/server flow, and legacy
  standalone sync docs.
- [Real-Time Sync Architecture](docs/realtime-sync/realtime-sync/architecture.md):
  deeper architecture for server/client sync pieces, WebSocket path, database
  change emission, and scaling considerations.
- [Real-Time Sync Wire Protocol](docs/realtime-sync/realtime-sync/protocol.md):
  wire message formats, sync snapshot/change/ack/catchup messages, mutation
  protocol, and reconnect behavior.
- [ReactiveDB Server Design](docs/realtime-sync/realtime-sync/reactive-db.md):
  server-side ReactiveDB internals, table definitions, transactions, change
  tracking, and SQLite behavior.
- [SyncStore Client Design](docs/realtime-sync/realtime-sync/sync-store.md):
  client-side store design, optimistic state, pending mutations, rollbacks,
  subscriptions, and React binding details.

### Platform Services

- [PDF Rendering](docs/pdf.md): managed Chromium setup, HTML/print CSS rendering,
  strict resource policy, limits, storage composition, workflows, stable
  errors/observability, deployment, and replaceable adapters.
- [Observability](docs/observability.md): observability event codes, sinks,
  frontend ingest, memory event store, protected event route, and how new logs,
  warnings, errors, and lifecycle events should flow.
- [Observability Audit](docs/observability-audit.md): historical
  pre-observability baseline; use the current Observability guide for runtime
  behavior.
- [Durable Workflow System](docs/workflows.md): workflow service, workflow
  registry, scheduled/background work concepts, app-facing usage, and future
  workflow expansion.
- [Webhooks Plan](docs/webhooks.md): planned inbound/outbound webhook system,
  signatures, workflow/table triggers, webhook delivery, and future API shape.

### Package, Release, And Maintenance

- [Releasing Zero](docs/releasing.md): package state, source-export strategy,
  current supported/preview boundary, package files, version bump, candidate
  verification, changelog, clean-checkout, commit, and tag checklist.
- [Zero Stabilization Plan](docs/stabilization-plan.md): historical record of
  the earlier local-create/package-mode stabilization pass; not a current
  release checklist.
- [Doctor Usage Audit Plan](docs/doctor-usage-audit-plan.md): source audit plan
  for warning agents about raw controls, custom modal/toast/sidebar systems,
  direct backend service bypasses, internal imports, missing root wiring, and
  route/policy shape issues.
